title: Exact Constant in the Independent-Set Asymptotic g(n) ~ c·n^{1/2} for Erdős Problem #1025

problemStatement.formal: g(n) = \min_{f \in \mathcal{F}_n} \max_{X \subseteq [n],\, X \text{ independent for } f} |X|, \quad \mathcal{F}_n = \{ f : \binom{[n]}{2} \to [n] : f(\{x,y\}) \notin \{x,y\} \}. \text{ Given } g(n) = \Theta(n^{1/2}), \text{ determine whether } c = \lim_{n \to \infty} g(n)/\sqrt{n} \text{ exists and its exact value.}
problemStatement.plain: Erdős Problem #1025 is solved up to constants: for any function f mapping each pair {x,y} of an n-element set to a third element (never x or y), one can always find an independent set X — one avoiding all values f({x,y}) for pairs inside X — of size on the order of sqrt(n), and this is optimal. Open: the exact constant. Does g(n)/sqrt(n) converge to a specific number c, and what is it? Spencer's lower bound and the Conlon–Fox–Sudakov upper bound leave a gap between their multiplicative constants.
whyMatters: Pinning the sharp constant is the natural step after the order of magnitude is known, and such constants (as in Ramsey/Turán/Zarankiewicz) are notoriously hard.
A matching constant would upgrade the qualitative Θ(n^{1/2}) into a genuine limit law and sharpen the link between Erdős–Hajnal set mappings and hypergraph independence.

knownResults: Spencer (1972): g(n) ≫ n^{1/2} via the deletion method.
Conlon–Fox–Sudakov (2016): g(n) ≪ n^{1/2}, giving g(n) = Θ(n^{1/2}).
references: P. Erdős and A. Hajnal, On the structure of set-mappings, Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. 9 (1958), 111–131.
J. Spencer, Turán's theorem for k-graphs, Discrete Math. 2 (1972), 183–186.
D. Conlon, J. Fox, B. Sudakov, extremal-combinatorics work (2016) — matching upper bound.
